The Hittite Empire. From 1650 to 1180 BCE, this was the ancient Near East's dominant power during the Bronze Age, centered on Anatolia—modern Turkey—and extending into Syria and Mesopotamia at its height. The Hittites pioneered iron-working technology, which gave them military advantage over bronze-using rivals. They also developed a sophisticated legal code and engaged in formal diplomatic treaties. The Treaty of Kadesh, negotiated in 1259 BCE between Hittite king Mursili II and Egyptian pharaoh Ramesses II, is the world's oldest recorded peace agreement.

The Hittites, an Indo-European people, migrated to Anatolia around 1700 BCE and gradually consolidated power, establishing their capital at Hattusa. The Old Hittite Kingdom, lasting from 1650 to 1450 BCE, saw repeated expansion into Syria and Mesopotamia. Kings like Mursili I reached as far as Babylon, though gains were rarely held. The New Hittite Kingdom, from 1450 to 1180 BCE, under Telepinu and later Mursili II, established a more stable feudal system of vassal states that could be held and taxed more effectively.

The Hittites pioneered iron smelting around 1500 BCE and incorporated iron into weaponry, giving them technological superiority over bronze-using rivals like Egypt and Assyria. The Hittite chariot corps, armed with iron-tipped spears and arrows, became a dominant force. The Chariot Manual, written by a Hittite named Kikkuli, is the oldest surviving treatise on military training. Hittite armies used coordinated formations and siege tactics that influenced later Near Eastern warfare.

The Code of Hammurabi heavily influenced Hittite law, but the Hittites developed a more sophisticated legal code emphasizing proportional justice, restitution over vengeance, and distinctions between classes of people. The Treaty of Kadesh, negotiated after the inconclusive Battle of Kadesh in 1274 BCE, established a boundary between Hittite and Egyptian spheres and ended a century of warfare. It is the oldest surviving international treaty and defined the model for diplomatic agreements. The Hittites maintained vassal states through a feudal system where subordinate rulers swore oaths of loyalty in exchange for protection and the right to govern locally. Rebellion was met with swift military punishment.

The Hittites adopted the gods of their Anatolian predecessors and incorporated deities from conquered territories, creating a syncretic pantheon that reflected their multi-ethnic empire. The royal family maintained religious authority, with the king serving as the intermediary between gods and subjects.

The New Hittite Kingdom collapsed around 1180 BCE in a period called the Bronze Age Collapse. Cities were destroyed and populations fled, possibly due to invasion by the Sea Peoples, famine, or internal conflict—the cause remains unclear. Hittite culture persisted in Neo-Hittite city-states in northern Syria that survived until the Assyrian conquest in the eighth century BCE.
